$comment: The contract between the browser and its own pages: every message a
page may send, and every path a page is served at.
generate_contract.py turns this into a TypeScript module and a C++
header. Neither side declares these names itself, because when they
were declared twice they went out of step -- thirteen messages existed
in TypeScript with no handler in C++, and Chromium answers an
unregistered chrome.send() by crashing the browser process.
Adding a message here is what makes it exist. Its handler still has to
be written, and the generated header lists it so the compiler asks.
Served at chrome://weglet/<path>. The names are also how the toolbar
recognises one of our own tabs, so they cannot live in two places.

$messages_comment: args is what the page sends, in order. Types are the TypeScript ones;
the C++ side receives them as a base::ListValue and validates each
itself -- a page is our own code, but it runs in a renderer, and a
compromised renderer is what this boundary is for.
`implemented: false` means the handler exists and only logs. It is
still registered, because an unregistered name crashes the browser.
The flag is what the generated header reports, so the gap is visible
$pushes_comment: The other direction: what the browser calls on a page.
WebUI pushes by calling a named function on a global, so each of these
is a name that has to be spelled the same in C++ and in TypeScript. It
was not: C++ called weglet.setNewTabState while the page installed
weglet.setNewTab, and the new tab page silently never received its
shortcuts. Nothing caught it, because this half of the contract was the
'page' is which page receives it, by the key from the pages block. That
is also what lets the browser push only to the pages a change concerns
instead of re-serialising everything to everyone.

$comment: The addresses the tab model (rust/weglet-core) knows as its own, in
the form the user sees them. Rust owns the literal strings -- see
weglet-core/src/lib.rs -- and this list has to name the same five,
because they were the same five once and drifted: three existed in
Rust with nothing on the C++ side to resolve them to a real page, so
a tab could carry a human label like 'Bookmarks' while the URL it
tried to load was a scheme the engine had never heard of.
'page' is which weglet:// page (from the pages block above) currently
stands in for this address. Several may point at newtab.html until
their own page exists -- that is a real product gap, not a bug, and
recorded here rather than silently absorbed into ResolveForEngine so
it stays visible.
